explanations.explanation: Incense it is. Israel burned fragrant incense on the altar every morning and again at twilight (Exodus 30:7-8). David, Israel's king, asks for his prayer to be set before the LORD "like incense." A sweet-smelling smoke rising up is the picture, and it sure beats my oven smell when I forget the timer.

Showbread was real, friend. Loaves were set out before the LORD each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-8). But David never mentions loaves here. He says his prayer is like incense, which goes up as smoke instead of sitting on a table.

Firstfruits were part of Israel's worship too, the first of the harvest brought to the priest (Leviticus 23:10). David doesn't reach for that picture in this psalm, though. He says his prayer should be set before the LORD "like incense." Good guess, baker, but that's a different part of the worship.

That's it. David prays, "Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips." The door of the lips is where words walk out. I think David knows how fast a word can leave once that door swings open.
Close, since ears are on the same face. But David talks about his mouth and the door of his lips. Words going out, not words coming in. The guard is posted where the talking happens.
David doesn't mention his feet or his route in this verse. He asks the LORD to "keep watch at the door of my lips." That's a door on the face, not a front door. So the guard stands at the mouth.
Heart is right. David prays, "Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing…" He's asking about the inside, where the pull starts, not only about what he does. That's a prayer worth stealing, baker.
Eyes show up later in this psalm, but not here. In verse 8 David's eyes are fixed on the LORD. In verse 4 it's his heart he asks the LORD not to let be drawn to any evil thing.
Feet don't appear in this verse. David says, "Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing…" The verse names the heart, not the feet.
Not quite, friend. David asks the opposite. He prays, "let me not feast on their delicacies." So he doesn't want to take part in their works, and he doesn't want to feast on their delicacies either.

False is right. David says, "let me not feast on their delicacies." He wants no share in the works of men who do iniquity, and no share in their treats either. I've turned down plenty of cookies in my day, but never because of who baked them, and this isn't about that.

A righteous man, yes. David says, "Let the righteous man strike me; let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." He's asking for a hard word from someone good. Not many people sign up for that, and I'd probably ask for a cookie first.

A Philistine giant is a David story, but not this one. Goliath, the Philistine giant, is in 1 Samuel 17, where David brings him down (1 Samuel 17:49-50). In this psalm David asks for "…the righteous man…" to strike him. Totally different kind of knock.

No Moabite king appears in this psalm. David says, "Let the righteous man strike me…" It's someone righteous he's asking for, not an enemy ruler. Good thing too, since you wouldn't want a king swinging by for a surprise visit.

That's right. David prays, "let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." He's asking for that rebuke to be an act of loving devotion, not an attack. Then he calls it "…oil for my head…" and I think that tells you how welcome it is.
David doesn't call it that. He says, "let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." Nothing about punishment or what he has earned. The text says love.
The psalm never says anything about a test of pride. David asks, "let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." It's love he names. Pride isn't in the verse.
True. Verse 5 ends, "For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked." Notice it says the deeds, not a list of names. David prays all the time against what the wicked do.

It's actually true. Verse 5 ends, "For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked." David says it right there in his own psalm. Easy to miss when the start of the verse has so much oil and striking going on.

Yes. David says, "When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs, the people will listen to my words…" So when those rulers fall, people turn their ears to him. It's a quiet room all of a sudden, and I'd love that for my kitchen.
Nobody flees the land in this verse. David says, "…the people will listen to my words…" The verse says listening, not fleeing.
The text goes the other direction. David says, "…the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant." They listen to him, not against him. Pleasant words, friend.

True. David says, "…the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant." The verse gives that reason right in the same breath. Pleasant words get listened to, and I wish my 'do not touch the cooling rack' talk were that pleasant.

It's true, baker. David says, "…the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant." The word pleasant is right there in verse 6. I know, it's a verse about rulers and cliffs, so it's easy to blink past that part.

Right. David says, "As when one plows and breaks up the soil, so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol." Soil broken up and turned over is the picture he uses. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be.
The wind and the chaff aren't in this verse. David says, "As when one plows and breaks up the soil…" His picture is plowing, not wind and chaff.
A potter and a jar don't show up in this psalm. The picture David uses is, "As when one plows and breaks up the soil…" It's farm work, not pottery. I think this one is a heavy verse.
Exactly. David says, "But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord." Even with a verse about scattered bones right before it, his eyes stay on God. That's the right place to look, baker.
David never mentions an army in this psalm. He says, "But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord." His eyes are on God, not on an army.
The hills aren't in this psalm. David says, "But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord." That's where he's looking. No scenery, just the LORD.

That's the one. David says, "In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless." He runs to the LORD for refuge and asks not to be left without defense. It's a plain, honest prayer, and I like those best.
Weary isn't in this verse. David asks, "do not leave my soul defenseless." He's asking about being protected, not about being tired. Different worry altogether.
David doesn't ask about being turned away. He says, "In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless." He seeks refuge in the LORD, and he asks not to be left defenseless.

Not quite, friend. David asks, "Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers." He asks to be kept from their traps, not to build any of his own. Then in verse 10 he says, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets…"

False is right. David asks God, "Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers." He wants to be kept out of the traps, not to set any himself. Then he says, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety."
Nets is right. David prays, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets…" The nets are theirs, not his. That's what he asks for the wicked.
Safety is right. The verse ends, "…while I pass by in safety." David isn't asking for a fight. He wants to walk right on past, unharmed.
Swords aren't in this verse. David says, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets…" Nets are what the wicked fall into. No blades in this one.
Silence doesn't fit this verse. David says he passes by "in safety." Silence is a nice idea, but he doesn't ask for it here. The verse is about getting past the traps unharmed.
Chains aren't in this psalm. David says, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety." The trap is a net. And I'd rather have him pass by in safety than in anything clanking.
